column1: In MLOps pipeline orchestration, what is the Dependency Invariant?
column2: A task T₂ may not begin execution until all tasks in predecessors(T₂) have reached a terminal success state.

column1: What is the Idempotency Invariant for pipeline tasks, and what does it require architecturally?
column2: Retrying a task must produce the same observable output as executing it once; this requires tasks to be side-effect-controlled — either purely functional or guarded by write-once artifact semantics.

column1: What is the valid state lattice for monotonic task state progression in a pipeline orchestrator?
column2: PENDING → QUEUED → RUNNING → {SUCCESS | FAILED | SKIPPED}. Backward transitions are not permitted without an explicit, auditable pipeline reset.

column1: Why must a pipeline dependency graph be acyclic (a DAG) rather than merely directed?
column2: Acyclicity is a liveness guarantee: a cycle creates deadlock (T_a waits on T_b, T_b waits on T_a, neither proceeds). Orchestrators must reject cycles at definition time via DFS-based coloring rather than deferring to runtime failure.

column1: What algorithms produce a valid topological ordering of a pipeline DAG, and what is their time complexity?
column2: Kahn's algorithm (1962) or DFS-based topological sort, both running in O(V + E) time, producing an ordering σ such that for every edge (u,v), σ(u) < σ(v).

column1: What determines the lower bound on a pipeline's wall-clock execution time, regardless of available resources?
column2: The critical path length — the length of the longest dependency chain from any source node to any sink node in the DAG.

column1: Why is monitoring a production ML system fundamentally different from monitoring a conventional web service?
column2: A web service is deterministic (same inputs → same outputs, correctness verifiable at deploy time). An ML model is stochastic and temporally unstable — it can appear healthy on infrastructure metrics while silently degrading in predictive quality as the world's statistics shift.

column1: What are the four independent failure axes in production ML systems?
column2: 1) Infrastructure failures (OOM, GPU ECC errors, crashes), 2) Data failures (inputs violate training distribution assumptions), 3) Model quality failures (concept drift — the learned f(x)→y becomes a stale approximation of true P(y|x)), 4) Operational failures (latency spikes, throughput degradation, cache inefficiencies).

column1: Why is alerting on mean shift alone insufficient for drift detection, per the Statistical Validity invariant?
column2: It misses variance explosions and multimodal distribution splits. Proper drift detection requires full distributional tests (KL divergence, PSI, KS test), not just threshold comparisons on point statistics.

column1: What is the distinction between feature drift and concept drift in ML monitoring?
column2: Feature drift (shift in input distribution) is a leading indicator; concept drift (the true mapping P(y|x) changing in the real world) is the lagging consequence — the model's learned function becomes a stale approximation.

column1: What is the 'artifact dependency graph' in MLOps, and why does it matter?
column2: It is the core data structure tracking every versioned dependency a serving model relies on: training dataset, feature engineering logic, preprocessing pipeline, model architecture, hyperparameters, and serving infrastructure. Any single component changing without re-validating the others can silently corrupt predictions.

column1: Why can identical training code and seeds produce different model accuracy across hardware topologies?
column2: Due to IEEE 754 floating-point non-associativity combined with non-deterministic reduction ordering in distributed collective operations (e.g., AllReduce over float16 via NCCL) — different hardware topologies or batch orderings yield different numerical results despite identical seeds and code.
